910.name: Celtic & Roman Alpine Settlements
910.description: The upper Rhine valley that would become Liechtenstein was inhabited by Celtic Raetian peoples before Roman conquest, incorporated into the province of Raetia with a Roman road station and small fort.

sub_clusters.name: Raetian Celtic Period
sub_clusters.description: Celtic Raetian hill settlements in the Alpine Rhine valley, pre-Roman trade routes, and the gradual expansion of Roman influence southward.

sub_clusters.name: Roman Raetia Presence
sub_clusters.description: Roman incorporation into Raetia, construction of road stations, small-scale Romanisation, and the eventual Alemannic settlement during the Migration Period.

920.name: Medieval Lordships & Holy Roman Empire
920.description: The territories of Vaduz and Schellenberg emerged as distinct lordships within the Holy Roman Empire, passing through multiple noble families before their eventual purchase by the Liechtenstein dynasty.

sub_clusters.name: County of Vaduz Origins
sub_clusters.description: Alemannic settlement, Christianisation, formation of the County of Vaduz and Lordship of Schellenberg under various Imperial noble families.

sub_clusters.name: Late Medieval Lordships
sub_clusters.description: The territories under the Counts of Werdenberg-Sargans and later the Counts of Sulz, experiencing the turmoil of late medieval Imperial politics.

930.name: Liechtenstein Dynasty Purchase & Imperial Status
930.description: The wealthy Liechtenstein family, seeking a seat in the Imperial Diet, purchased Schellenberg (1699) and Vaduz (1712), which Emperor Charles VI elevated to the Principality of Liechtenstein in 1719.

sub_clusters.name: Early Modern Lordship & Wars
sub_clusters.description: The territories during the Reformation, Thirty Years' War devastation, witch trials, and the impoverishment that led the Hohenems counts to sell their lands.

sub_clusters.name: Creation of the Principality (1719)
sub_clusters.description: Anton Florian von Liechtenstein's purchase of Schellenberg (1699) and Vaduz (1712), and the imperial elevation to a principality by Charles VI on 23 January 1719.
key_events: Emperor Charles VI creates the Principality of Liechtenstein (23 January 1719)

940.name: Napoleonic Sovereignty & German Confederation
940.description: Napoleon's dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire paradoxically granted Liechtenstein full sovereignty. The principality navigated the Confederation of the Rhine and German Confederation while remaining a tiny agrarian state.

sub_clusters.name: Confederation of the Rhine & Sovereignty
sub_clusters.description: Liechtenstein gains sovereignty through membership in Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine (1806), ending feudal subordination and beginning its existence as an independent state.
key_events: Liechtenstein gains sovereignty via the Confederation of the Rhine (1806)

sub_clusters.name: German Confederation Membership
sub_clusters.description: Liechtenstein in the German Confederation, the first princely visit to the territory (1842), abolition of serfdom, and the decision not to join either Austria or Prussia after 1866.

940.name: Swiss Alignment & Early Modernisation
940.description: After the dissolution of the German Confederation, Liechtenstein oriented toward Switzerland, abolishing its army in 1868 and beginning cautious modernisation under Prince Johann II, the longest-reigning monarch.

sub_clusters.name: Army Abolition & Swiss Turn
sub_clusters.description: Abolition of the military (1868), diplomatic representation via Austria-Hungary, Prince Johann II's 70-year reign, and the beginnings of Swiss economic alignment.

950.name: World Wars & Swiss Customs Union
950.description: Liechtenstein's pivot from Austria to Switzerland during and after WWI, formalised through the 1924 customs union, and its careful maintenance of neutrality during WWII despite Nazi pressure.

sub_clusters.name: WWI & Swiss Customs Union
sub_clusters.description: Economic hardship during WWI, collapse of the Austria-Hungary connection, adoption of the Swiss franc, and the landmark customs and monetary union with Switzerland (1924).

sub_clusters.name: WWII Neutrality & Nazi Pressure
sub_clusters.description: Liechtenstein's precarious neutrality during WWII, the Anschluss next door, a failed Nazi putsch attempt, and the principality's acceptance of a Russian Liberation Army unit's surrender in 1945.

960.name: Financial Centre & Modern Microstate
960.description: Liechtenstein's transformation from a poor agrarian territory to one of the world's wealthiest states per capita through industrialisation, banking, and financial services, alongside constitutional debates and European integration.

sub_clusters.name: Postwar Industrialisation & Banking
sub_clusters.description: Rapid industrialisation (Hilti, Ivoclar), development as a financial centre with favourable tax and banking secrecy laws, and growing international scrutiny.

sub_clusters.name: EEA Membership & Constitutional Reform
sub_clusters.description: Joining the EEA (1995), UN membership (1990), Prince Hans-Adam II's controversial 2003 constitutional reform expanding princely powers, and ongoing adaptation of financial regulations to international standards.
key_events: Liechtenstein joins the European Economic Area (1995)
Constitutional reform expands princely powers via referendum (2003)
